title: The big lookout
hook: look back down the hill: from salaam on day one to a whole juz' carried in the heart

segments.voice: Yesterday, what year one gave: five camps, and five lines. Your line was a year of remembering. Which line did you most want to carry forward? Day three hundred thirty-one.

You know the moment on a long hike when the trees thin out and suddenly you can see. The trail you've been staring at for hours turns out to be a thin line winding up from a valley you'd almost forgotten. You can see the town where you started. And ahead, a further range you didn't know was there. Stand here a minute. This is the last day of camp five, and the last day of year one. Today: the big lookout.
screen: `THE TREES THIN OUT.` → `THE TOWN WHERE YOU STARTED.` → `A FURTHER RANGE AHEAD.`

segments.voice: Look back down the hill. Way down there, day one: salaam. Then bismillah before every beginning, alhamdulillah as a reflex. You learned the Fatiha one piece at a time, before you knew what a juz' was. You walked with the prophets, Ibrahim leaving home, Yusuf in the well, Yunus in the dark, and then with the Prophet ﷺ, from the cave to the camel kneeling in Medina. You learned what the body does in prayer and what the fingers do in dhikr. Then you walked the thirtieth part of the Qur'an backward, from An-Nas to An-Naba', the way children all over the world do. A whole juz', carried in the heart, or at least begun there. Then camp five took you further in: the names, from the Merciful to the Patient; Medina and the farewell sermon; the Sufi path for those who took it; and how the book itself was built, from palm stalks to the dots over the letters to a voice heard at every dawn. That's this camp closing, and year one with it. Now look ahead. Year two is the book, surah by surah: starting from the Opening and al-Baqarah and reading onward, a little each day, all the way to the edge of the juz' you already know. It's a big range. But you've already done the hardest part of any climb: you kept coming back. The Prophet said, as Bukhari records, that the deeds most loved by Allah are the ones done regularly, even if they're small. That's how this hill was climbed. One small day at a time, from salaam to here. From here you can see.
screen: `LOOK BACK DOWN THE HILL` · `A WHOLE JUZ', BEGUN IN THE HEART` · `CAMP FIVE: FURTHER IN` · `AHEAD: THE BOOK, SURAH BY SURAH`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: recite your verse, then rest. Choose the verse that stayed with you most this year: the one you wrote on paper, a line of al-Fatiha, al-Kawthar, or bismillah itself. Say it once, aloud, slowly, the way you'd speak at the top of a hill. Then stop. Don't do anything else. Sit, rest, and let the whole year lie behind you like a view. If you pray, you can thank Allah in your own words. The bell holds the time.
The big lookout. The top of year one: the path you climbed, from salaam to a juz' in the heart, and the book still ahead. Today's word.
Your line: from here you can see. Today, tell one person one thing you learned this year, just one, and notice how far you've come. Tomorrow, year two begins. Day three hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Many Muslims keep a small daily portion of Qur'an reading and remembrance rather than occasional long sessions, following the teaching that the deeds most loved by Allah are the regular ones, even if small.

fork.reveal: rest, then keep going: the deeds most loved are the regular ones, even if small. year two is the whole book.

original.note: Arabic: peace. the path's first word, from the same root as Islam and Muslim.

trapdoor: what you thought: the end of the course.
what it means: a lookout: a place to see the whole climb, and the range still ahead.
what a scholar hears: the teaching in Bukhari that the most beloved deeds are the most regular, even if few: the method of the whole path.
